name: Pax Silica still has to make its case
desc: The Philippines has offered public land for a US-backed tech hub. Filipinos still need the exact boundaries and final terms, and the case for technology should start with funding Filipino science.

p: On September 1, the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) denied a freedom of information request for the exact boundaries of the proposed Pax Silica hub in New Clark City. The request asked for the site's corner coordinates and a map of the lots inside it. BCDA cited the exception for prejudicial premature disclosure and replied, "The information is withheld temporarily until the official action is finalized or published."[1]
That's documented withholding of information. The government is asking for our support before we can check exactly which land it plans to commit.

The Philippines joined Pax Silica, the US-led initiative on AI supply chains, on April 16. Trade USec Ceferino Rodolfo signed the declaration in Washington, and both countries announced plans that day for a 4,000-acre industrial hub in the Luzon Economic Corridor.[2] Rodolfo himself calls Pax Silica a partnership founded on "a non-binding statement of shared principles among trusted partners."[3]

In a letter dated April 9, BCDA offered the US two rent-free years on that land, about 1,619 hectares of New Clark City. The Philippine Embassy sent the proposal to the State Department on April 16. Rent from the third year onward and the exact boundaries were left for later agreements.[4]

As of November 18, the framework agreement for the Clark hub, the document that should spell out what each side commits to, was still unsigned.[5][6] That day, during Donald Trump's state visit, President Marcos said, "There is no signing. Not on this trip."[7]

BCDA estimates US$40 billion to US$70 billion in investment and 130,000 to 190,000 jobs once the hub is fully developed.[5] Diversified export markets and skilled employment are real possibilities, and some of that could happen. But they're potential benefits, not guaranteed outcomes. The published documents give estimates. They don't say how many of those jobs must go to Filipinos or what investors would be legally bound to deliver.
So the Philippines could commit public land and waive two years of rent on it without securing proportionate, enforceable benefits for Filipinos.

BCDA has shown a concept map of the site.[8] In September, it withheld the exact boundary and parcel data the requester sought.[1] Human Rights Watch (HRW) noted in its November 16 report that BCDA "has not provided a detailed map." An independent map cited by HRW places the Aeta community of Sapang Kawayan inside the estimated site boundary.[6]

The government also hasn't published a cost-benefit analysis for the hub. Researchers at UP Los Baños wrote their own assessment and called for more study before any irreversible commitment.[9] The public materials still leave a basic question unanswered. What would the Philippines give up, and what would it get in return? At a UP Diliman forum in October, biologist Jelaine Gan cited BCDA's estimate that the development would need 65 to 90 million liters of water a day.[10] Where would that much water come from, and what would it cost to supply?

On August 26, Acting Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna told the House, "There has been no environmental impact assessment applied for or processed," and said DENR didn't have a clear project description to assess.[11] DENR issued a clearance for the wider New Clark City development plan in 2019. Projects locating in the hub would still need their own.[11][12]
BCDA's proposal says the planned coordination office would support training and technology transfer.[4] It leaves open what companies would have to share, and with whom.

HRW reports that the Aeta Hungey community in Sapang Kawayan, Capas, first sought recognition of its ancestral domain in 1994 and still had no title as of November 16. HRW says the available information indicates BCDA never secured the community's free, prior and informed consent.[6] The Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act (RA 8371) requires prior certification from the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples before the government can grant a covered lease. If the project overlaps an ancestral domain, the commission generally requires the affected community's free, prior and informed consent in writing.[13] BCDA says it holds title to the land and that the site is in an area designated for development.[8] The public map doesn't establish whether the final site overlaps the community's claim. "We do not want to give up our community," the tribe's chieftain, Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, told HRW.[6]

Farmers in Sitio Binyayan, Barangay O'Donnell, told HRW that BCDA offered compensation of ₱300,000 per hectare of affected farmland. The barangay head, Wendell Mercado, said some were given 30 days to answer and some only 10. He and the Capas mayor asked BCDA for a public consultation. "To this day, we are still waiting," he said.[6]

sections.h: And the burden of proof rests on whom?
p: We don't need to prove that Pax Silica will harm the Philippines to justify opposing it. The government should have to show that the benefits outweigh the costs and risks, not the other way around. Given how large this project's effects could be, good or bad, the missing information alone is reason enough to oppose it as it stands.
Don't get it wrong, this isn't an argument against industrialization or foreign investment. It's an argument for informed democratic consent and government accountability.

sections.h: But... what about the jobs and opportunities it generates?
p: I frankly don't understand the pro-Pax Silica people who lean on the argument of "technological advancement" and "jobs for Filipinos." I think it's very tone-deaf.

If you believe technology is what will finally industrialize the Philippines, where were you when our own science sector was being starved? DOST's latest compendium puts national R&D spending, across all sectors, at 0.32% of GDP in 2018. By 2022, the last year in that series, it was 0.19%.[14] Our own development plan targets 1% by 2028.[15]

By the count of the scientists' group AGHAM, the government's R&D budget fell from ₱20.3 billion in 2022 to ₱18.2 billion in 2024.[16] DOST's own appropriations did grow each year in that stretch.[17] For 2025, the Philippine News Agency reported that DOST asked for ₱49.25 billion.[18] The executive's budget proposal gave it ₱28.46 billion.[19] Congress enacted ₱28.68 billion, about 58% of the request.[17]

DOST's compendium calls for "more competitive compensation to attract and retain researchers."[14] A 2020 ILO report linked Filipino scientists' decisions to work abroad to low pay and weak research incentives.[20] Our scientists are underpaid, our labs are underfunded, and some of our best researchers leave. None of that moved pro-Pax Silica people, but a US-backed hub in Tarlac suddenly makes you a champion of innovation?

Rodolfo says BOI is working with UP and other universities on research and training around New Clark City.[3] Good. Then the question therefore is what the companies at the hub will actually commit to doing with them.

Technological advancement isn't something another country installs on our land. It is something we build, with our own scientists and our own research. You can want foreign investment and strong local science at the same time. But I implore you to say both; demand both. Fund DOST, fund our universities, pay our researchers. If you're really pro-technology, be pro-Filipino science first.
Progress that skips our own scientists isn't really ours. It only happens to be located here.
